title: Tortilla Chips 300g

drivers.name: Price increase +3.7%
drivers.evidence: Past price hikes (e.g., 2026-09-28) caused ~20% drop; new price is higher than any prior, and competitor entry amplifies sensitivity.

drivers.name: New competitor across the street
drivers.evidence: Planner note suggests competitive threat; no past data, but plausible demand loss in high-competition snack category.

adjustment.analysis: Halloween historically lowers sales (x0.79 median vs baseline, noise-adjusted x1.0), but the baseline already reflects this trend. The price increase to $3.97 (+3.7%) is likely to reduce demand, especially with a new competitor opening across the street. Past promotions show average uplift of x1.82, but this week has no promotion. The price hike and new competition are credible demand reducers. Evidence is limited (one past Halloween effect, no past price increase at this level), so shrink toward 1.0. No promotion, so no uplift. Adjust down for price and competition.

brief:

TARGET WEEK: 2026-10-26 to 2026-11-01 (3 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: Holiday: Halloween (Sat)
  shelf price: 3.97 (+3.7% vs regular price 3.83)
  planner notes: A competitor opens a store across the street this week

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 124.2 | 5%-95%: 77.6 - 200.2 | 10%-90%: 89.0 - 170.1

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-29% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
